feedback: If the learner says 'the elephant is grieving' from behaviour alone, ask what observation would distinguish grief from another cause, and what simpler explanation should be ruled out first.
If the learner treats passing the mirror test as proof of overall intelligence, point out it tests one ability — self-recognition — not intelligence in general.

When the learner proposes marking the animal and checking whether it uses the mirror to investigate the mark on its OWN body, affirm that this is the mirror mark test scientists use as evidence of self-recognition, and ask what controls help, such as a mark it cannot feel and comparing behaviour with and without the mirror.
If the learner ranks the animals, press them to say in what life-fitted way each is clever rather than which is 'smarter'.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating evidence from assumption is the scientific habit here: a behaviour that looks like a human feeling needs a designed test and the ruling-out of simpler explanations before we claim an animal understands.
learnerActions: Pick a clever animal behaviour to discuss — an elephant that seems to mourn, a crow bending a wire into a hook, a dolphin at a mirror.
Describe what is actually observed (not what you assume the animal feels).

Face the challenge question: 'That's what it looks like to us — but how could we test whether the animal understands, or whether it's trial-and-error, or whether we're just seeing our own feelings in it?'
Propose a concrete test: mark the animal and show it a mirror; give it a puzzle it could not have been born knowing how to solve.
State what a single positive result shows (one specific ability) and what it does NOT show (general intelligence).
activities.title: How do you KNOW? Questioning a cognition scientist

feedback: If a learner reads a mirror response as the animal 'liking looking at itself', clarify that the mark test shows self-recognition only when the animal uses the mirror to investigate a mark on its own body.
If a learner concludes a single test proves overall intelligence, redirect: it demonstrates one ability.
When a learner demands a repeat or a control to rule out luck or instinct in the trial-and-error scenario, affirm this is good scientific reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Each test probes one specific ability; a result must be interpreted carefully, and apparent insight can sometimes be explained by simpler processes unless further evidence rules them out.
learnerActions: Run a mirror mark test on a species: place a mark the animal cannot feel where it cannot see it directly, present the mirror, and observe whether the animal uses the reflection to investigate the mark on its own body more than it touches that spot without the mirror.
Run a puzzle box or multi-step problem on a different species and watch how it works out a solution.
Record a conclusion for each test: what ability the result demonstrates, and what it does not.
Sort behaviours into 'evidence' (what the behaviour actually shows) versus 'assumption' (what we merely imagine the animal feels).
Meet a trick scenario where trial-and-error or luck mimics insight, and decide what further evidence you would demand before concluding the animal 'understands'.
activities.title: Test the mind: running and interpreting experiments

feedback: If a learner says the octopus is 'less intelligent' because it is less like a human, reframe: octopus puzzle-solving and chimp tool-use are different kinds of intelligence, not higher and lower.
If a learner dismisses crows or octopuses as unintelligent because their brains are small or different, cite the hard puzzles they solve despite very different brains.
If a learner calls all animal problem-solving 'just instinct', contrast fixed instinct with flexible learned solutions — a crow bending a new wire into a hook, meerkats teaching pups.

Reinforce that an octopus is brilliant at physical puzzles and at working out escape routes (helped by its boneless, colour-changing body), while a chimp excels at tools and complex social life: each is clever in the ways its survival needs.
activities.intendedInsight: Intelligence takes different forms suited to each species' life; it is not a single ladder with humans at the top, and brain size alone does not decide it.
learnerActions: Gather varied examples across tool use (chimp, crow), problem-solving (octopus opening a jar, escaping a tank), memory, communication, social learning and teaching (meerkats teaching pups to handle scorpions), and self-recognition (dolphin, plus the debated magpie and elephant cases).
Match each animal to the kind of intelligence it shows, and to the way its own life makes that ability useful.
Compare an octopus, a crow, and a dolphin and explain how each is clever in a different, life-fitted way.
Answer: a pigeon has a tiny brain but can recognise hundreds of pictures — does brain size decide intelligence? Give a reason.
Explain why ranking species on a single 'smartness' line below humans is the wrong model.
activities.title: Different kinds of clever — not one ladder
